summary.en: Transit reduces air pollution and makes everyone healthier! People who use transit get more three times the amount of physical activity per day than those who don’t. Austin is full…

image.alt: Three individuals sitting at a Bus stop bench, smiling at each other.

body.text: Transit reduces air pollution and makes everyone healthier! People who use transit get more three times the amount of physical activity per day than those who don’t. Austin is full of frequent transit options that will get you where you are headed. Austin’s convenient bus and train system is continuing to expand with new service areas and stops. Leave the driving to someone else and focus on the fun times at your destination.

[CapMetro](https://www.capmetro.org/): Use [CapMetro’s](https://www.capmetro.org/) local routes to get you around Austin during the day and late into the night. Plan your transit trip using CapMetro’s [Trip Planner Tool](https://capmetro.org/planner/). Download the [CapMetro App](https://capmetro.org/app/) to digitally purchase a ticket and follow [@CapMetroATX](https://x.com/CapMetroATX) for the latest updates.

[High-Frequency Bus](https://www.capmetro.org/high-frequency): To get you around all parts of Austin fast and conveniently, CapMetro offers 14 routes that operate every 15 minutes between 6 a.m. and 8 p.m. every day of the week. See the [High-Frequency Map](https://www.capmetro.org/docs/default-source/plan-your-trip-docs/destination-schedule-book-docs/high-frequency-map.pdf?sfvrsn=dca6_8)

[CapMetro Rail](https://www.capmetro.org/redline): Use the CapMetro Rail to commute in for work or events —it runs from downtown to Leander. The Downtown Station has opened, situated in front of the Convention Center. Single ride is $3.50, Day Pass is $7.

[Park & Rides](https://www.capmetro.org/using-parknrides): Park & Ride facilities covering the North, South, East, and West let you transform a frustrating drive into a relaxing, productive ride. See [Park & Ride Map](https://www.capmetro.org/docs/default-source/plan-your-trip-docs/destination-schedule-book-docs/park-ride-station-locations.pdf?sfvrsn=e6626fba_14).

[Interurban Coach](http://www.ridecarts.com/services/interurban): Intercity [CARTS](http://www.ridecarts.com/) routes provide connections between Austin and select locations — Bastrop, Georgetown, Liberty Hill, Round Rock, Texas State University, Smithville, and more. This service conveniently connects to Greyhound and CapMetro.

summary.en: Ever wonder what you can and can’t do on the bus or rail, or just common etiquette when riding? Here’s a quick 101 on transit etiquette.

image.alt: Lady in pink and white dress smiling making a peace sign with their hand as they board the CapMetro Bus

body.text: Ever wonder what you can and can’t do on the bus or rail, or just common etiquette when riding? Here’s a quick 101 on transit etiquette:

items: Let folks exit the vehicle before you board.
Scan or pay your fare at the front when boarding.
If you have a mobile pass, scan your pass at the reader at the front (you often have to hold it further away from the camera than you think).
You can also swipe a physical transit card or pay with exact change (this is near the bus driver in front of their separator.

Always leave the front seats for those who need them, including folks with disabilities and seniors. If you feel it’s a full bus and you feel it’s appropriate, offer your seat to someone who needs it more than you.
Keep your things in your lap.
Don’t eat or drink (other than water) on the vehicles. If you have food or drink, make sure it’s in a spill-proof container.
When boarding and exiting, watch your step and do not cross in front of the vehicle.
Yes, the train has WiFi! It’s free and available to all riders.
Pets, emotional support and comfort animals are not allowed on CapMetro vehicles. Service animals are permitted.

body.text: Check out the [full bus rules and etiquette on the CapMetro website here](https://www.capmetro.org/rules).

title.en: How to Put Your Bike on the Bus

summary.en: If you’ve been too scared to try and put your bike on the bus, this is for you. It’s easier than you think. Here’s a step-by-step on how to do it.

image.alt: Individual putting a White Bike on to the Cap Metro Bus Bike Rack

body.text: If you’ve been too scared to try and put your bike on the bus, this is for you. It’s easier than you think. Here’s a step-by-step on how to do it:

items: Squeeze the handle to pull the rack down.
Load your bike (it’s better to load your bike on the closest rack to the bus in case anyone else needs to load after you).
Pull the handle over the front tire.
You’re done!

body.text: When you remove your bike, don’t forget to squeeze the handle to put the rack back up. If you need help, never hesitate to ask your bus driver for help!

Check out CapMetro’s website for a [video tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ERDa0_0GiFQ) or [check out our Instagram post](https://www.instagram.com/p/C2iueXyNKf_/?img_index=1) for a photo guide. [Plan your CapMetro trip here](https://www.capmetro.org/planner).
Ride safe, folks! ✨

summary.en: Take your bike’s “ABC Quick Check,” inspect your helmet and wear appropriate clothing to ensure you have a safe trip on two wheels.

image.alt: Individual standing and smiling in front of the "How YOU doin" mural with yellow bike and helmet

items: Take your bike’s “ABC Quick Check” – check the **A**ir, **B**rakes, **C**ranks and **C**hains, and quick releases.

Inspect your helmet for a proper fit and strap fit. The unbuttoned helmet should be level and two fingers wide above the eyebrows, with only a small movement when shaking from side to side. The side straps should come to a point just below the ears. The chin strap should reach approximately one-half inch below the chin with the mouth closed.
Wear clothing that can protect you from the elements, be seen by drivers, and fits snugly to prevent skin irritation and chain snagging.
Adjust the height, angle and handlebar of the bike seat for comfort.
Learn to change gears in various degrees and to make driving easier. Always shift into a comfortable starting gear before stopping.
Use good bicycle manners: announce as you pass; yield when entering and crossing; Stay to the right; pass by the left; the hand signal turns and stops; and use lights at night.

summary.en: ANYONE CAN BIKE IN AUSTIN CapMetro Bikeshare (formerly MetroBike) is Austin’s affordable and sustainable bikeshare system consisting of a fleet of 100% electric bikes at more than 75 stations available…

image.alt: Three individuals smiling as they check out three metro bikes from a bikeshare station

body.text: ANYONE CAN BIKE IN AUSTIN

CapMetro Bikeshare (formerly MetroBike) is Austin’s affordable and sustainable bikeshare system consisting of a fleet of 100% electric bikes at more than 75 stations available 24/7 that connect to CapMetro’s bus and rail routes. Rent out a Bikeshare at one station, ride it around town, and then check it back in at any other location. Use the [CapMetro Bikeshare app](https://capmetro.org/app/) or check the [bikeshare stations map](https://www.capmetro.org/bikeshare-stations) for the nearest stations to you. This program is owned and operated by CapMetro and the City of Austin.

items: Rent
Before you get riding you’ll need to purchase a pass or membership through one of our many options.
CapMetro Bikeshare App: [iPhone](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/capmetro-bikeshare-app/id6535647192) | [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.lyft.android.austinapp)
[Apply for a Student Pass](https://app.capmetro.org/BikeSharePassUTAndHT?_ga=2.160557053.1969918355.1729643941-1421482511.1728047205)
University of Texas at Austin students and staff: $12 per year
Huston-Tillotson University student and staff: Free
The kiosks
Ride
Checkout a bike from any station around town and feel the breeze in your hair!
[Station map](https://www.capmetro.org/bikeshare-stations)
Use any of the following to checkout our bike:
CapMetro Bikeshare App: [iPhone](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/capmetro-bikeshare-app/id6535647192) | [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.lyft.android.austinapp)
The kiosk
RFID card
Return
In order to end your current trip you MUST return the bicycle to a dock without exception.
Single-use pass holders will need to purchase another pass in order to checkout another bicycle. To stop the clock, dock!
Multi-use pass or membership holders can continue to checkout bikes until their access to the system expires. To reset the clock, dock!
When returning a bicycle you will hear the dock beep letting you know the locks are engaging. Once beeps finish pull on the bike to ensure it is secure.
If you have trouble with a dock accepting the bike, try a different available dock.
Station full? Go to the kiosk, click start, then click more options, then click full station. This will add ride time giving you just enough time to find another station with available docks.
Repeat
Depending on your pass or membership level, most users have an unlimited number of 60 minute trips included for the length of their access period.
Single-use passes have no limit on trip length but require that you purchase another pass once you have ended your current trip.
Multi-use pass or membership holders may use the kiosk or CapMetro Bikeshare app to checkout bikes for additional trips.
The bike from your most recent trip MUST be returned properly before the system will allow you to checkout another bike.

summary.en: Bike theft is a problem in many cities and we’re here to provide tips on how to secure your precious wheels.

image.alt: Individual putting on a helmet with a blue electric bike in front of the Cap Metro Bike Shelter- Sign reads Metro Bike Card, Keeps your bike safe in this secure facility

body.alt: Individual putting on a helmet with a blue electric bike in front of the Cap Metro Bike Shelter- Sign reads Metro Bike Card, Keeps your bike safe in this secure facility

body.text: We want to make it easier for you to start your first bike trip, and that means making the end just as easy. Parking your bike and feeling confident that it is securely stored is crucial for an enjoyable trip.
**Preventing theft:**
Bike theft is a problem in many cities and we’re here to provide tips on how to secure your precious wheels.

items: Park in an area where there is heavy foot traffic and eyes on the bike rack.
Lock your frame and the front wheel to the rack using a U-lock. Bonus points if you have a cable to also lock your rear wheel.

If leaving your bike for an extended period of time, find a secured facility. Your apartment or workplace may have a secured bike facility that is only accessible to people with access to the building.

body.text: **Parking your bike:**
The City of Austin requires many new developments to provide bike parking. If you find a location in need of bike parking, you can help get the wheels turning.
The City of Austin’s [Active Transportation Program](http://austintexas.gov/activetransportation) helps install free bike parking within the public right of way.

items: U-racks can be installed onto existing concrete within the right of way. A U-rack can provide parking for up to two bicycles.
Bike corrals repurpose a vehicle parallel parking spot with an on-street bicycle parking facility. Bike corrals may accommodate 6-14 bicycles.

body.text: The City of Austin is taking applications for additional bicycle locations throughout Austin’s core. Please read and follow the guidelines, then download and fill out an application.

items: [Bicycle parking guidelines](https://www.austintexas.gov/sites/default/files/files/Transportation/Bicycle_Parking_FAQ.pdf) (PDF)
[Bicycle parking digital application](https://atd.knack.com/atd-forms#bike-parking-application/)

body.text: Requests are evaluated based upon available right of way space, bicycle parking demand and availability of nearby bicycle parking. If you are a resident requesting bicycle parking, you must obtain support from the business owner and provide contact information. Requested locations will be evaluated by City of Austin staff. Bicycle parking is installed at selected locations in the public right of way and at no cost to the business owner.

summary.en: Wearing a helmet is one of the most important things you can do when riding a bike. A helmet protects your head, and inside your head is your brain —…

image.alt: Smiling rider in an orange bike helmet holding up five fingers on a trail in Austin

body.text: Wearing a helmet is one of the most important things you can do when riding a bike. A helmet protects your head, and inside your head is your brain — the part of you that controls your thoughts, personality and everything you do. Keeping your brain safe keeps you safe.
It is the law in Austin for anyone under 18 to wear a helmet when riding a bike.
Follow these steps to make sure your helmet fits the right way.

items.title: Find the Front of Your Helmet
text: Hold the helmet in front of you at your belly button like a bowl. Make sure the straps are hanging out, not twisted and the front of the helmet is facing your belly button. Then place the helmet on your head.

items.title: Position the Helmet Correctly
text: Your helmet shouldn’t sit too far back or too far forward.
If it’s too far back, your forehead isn’t protected.
If it’s too far forward, you can’t see where you’re going.
To find the right spot, place two fingers above your eyebrows. Lower the helmet until the bottom edge touches your fingers. That’s the correct position.

items.title: Tighten the Back
text: Make a “claw” with three fingers and reach for the adjustment knob on the back of the helmet.
The helmet should feel snug. When you shake your head, it shouldn’t move or fall off.

items.title: Check the Straps
text: Make two peace signs with your hands. Place your fingers around the straps near your ears. The straps should form a “V” shape with your ear in the middle.

items.title: Buckle Up
text: Finally, buckle the chin strap. It should be snug but comfortable — you should be able to fit two fingers between the strap and your chin.

body.text: Check out the videos covering the 5 Steps of Helmet Fitting:
[5 Steps of Helmet Fitting – Ghisallo Cycling Education](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GdiiVwK9rZg)
[Get There ATX- Instagram Post](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DTvv2vJkYZC/?igsh=dDByZWE2dHczaGV5)

summary.en: As the new school year begins, many families are adjusting their daily routines to fit in school drop-offs and pick-ups. We put together a list of local resources and safety tips to help you Get There to and from school.

image.alt: Middle school student using protected bike lane, school bus in the background going the opposite direction as the student rider

body.alt: Middle school student using protected bike lane, school bus in the background going the opposite direction as the student rider

body.text: As the new school year begins, many families are adjusting their daily routines to fit in school drop-offs and pick-ups. Whether you’re juggling work schedules, extracurriculars, or just trying to beat the morning rush, figuring out the best way to get your kids to school can often feel like a puzzle. To make things easier, we’ve created a quick guide to **help you explore safe, sustainable, and timely transportation option**s for your family. But this isn’t just about logistics—it’s about creating healthier communities, happier kids, and smoother mornings for everyone.
Beyond getting your kids to school, the transportation options listed below offer additional benefits, including:
Reducing traffic congestion and vehicle speed near schools
Minimizing cars and speed to under 25 miles per an hour around campuses creates safer streets for students, reduces drop-off delays, and calms the neighborhood traffic.
Decreasing air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions
Fewer vehicles idling around a school for drop-off or pick-ups helps to improve local air quality and protects students from high levels of exposure to vehicle emissions.
Enhancing academic performance and behavior
The brain is the muscle that benefits the most from biking or walking in the morning, whether it is a 20-minute walk or a 3-minute race to school, students feel better prepared to start the day!
Promoting peer and social interaction
Whether it’s riding the bus, walking, or carpooling with friends, being with others encourages students to disconnect from technology and reconnect with their peers.
Teaching safe walking, biking, and transit habits
Just like learning how to walk and talk is a learned skill, **knowing what safe traveling habits are— needs to be taught and practiced.**
Fostering neighborhood connections and community building
By ensuring our students are able to safely navigate their neighborhood, we are able to prioritize using human-power, making their space safe for them and everyone in the neighborhood.
Encouraging independence and self-confidence in students
Using active or shared transportation can improve mood, self-esteem, and reduce the stress on both the parent and students.
Growing an active and healthy lifestyle

Students who use active transportation or park and walk/roll methods begin to form regular physical activity habits— that start to lead them to choose to walk, bike, carpooling, and/or public transit as they grow.
Transportation Options for School Aged Children and Teens
Walking, Biking, or Scooting

body.alt: Group of elementary student riders using the protected bike lanes during Purple Sages's Bike to School Day

body.text: Tips:

items: For younger students, plan and practice a route with your child beforehand. Confidence in navigating a route to school is built over time and is a learned behavior.

Teach your student [safe riding](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dkoVxBnnGko) and [street crossing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gSlkn21915M) techniques. Check the weather to make sure your student is appropriately dressed and hydrated.
Pack sunscreen in your student’s backpack for reapplication for the way home.

body.text: Riding the School Bus or CapMetro Bus

body.alt: Parent and child getting off a Cap Metro Bus, two cyclists using the red bike lane.

body.text: Tips:

items: Review AISD school bus routes and CapMetro bus routes to determine the best route for your child.
If your child has never ridden a school bus before, take them to the bus stop before school starts to familiarize them with the pick-up and drop-off location.

If your child has never ridden a CapMetro bus before, practice their route with them before school starts. Get on with them at the bus stop and get off at their destination. Take the route the opposite way to practice the trip home.
**Kids age 18 and younger ride CapMetro for free!** Children 10 years and younger must be accompanied by someone 12 or older.
Remind your child not to run or play while they are waiting for the bus.
Always plan to arrive five minutes before the bus is scheduled to arrive.
Review school bus safety rules and public transit etiquette with your child.
Consider taking turns chaperoning the bus stop with other parents.

[**AISD School Bus Behavior Rules**](https://www.austinisd.org/transportation/guidelines#:~:text=Behavior%20Rules%3A%20Respect%20Self%2C%20Others,assign%20seats%20at%20any%20time) – School bus rules and disciplinary action

body.text: Tips:

items: Talk to other parents at your kid’s school to discuss carpooling opportunities
Organize a carpool, including dates, times, pickup/drop off locations
Ensure you and your student(s) are ready on time for the carpool
Provide advanced notice if things change
Be courteous and respectful of others
Always plan to arrive five minutes before the bus is scheduled to arrive.
Remind your student(s) not to leave trash or your belongings in another person’s vehicle

body.text: Austin’s New Bike Bus Program

body.alt: Group of elementary student riders using the protected bike lanes during Purple Sages's Bike to School Day
Blurred photo of student rider in front of a group students participating in a Bike Bus
Middle school student using protected bike lane, school bus in the background going the opposite direction as the student rider

body.text: Austin Bike Bus Program – Overview

Austin’s Bike Bus Program is a fun, safe, and community-powered way for students to bike to school in guided group rides led by trained adults. These rides help students build healthy habits, improve focus, gain independence, reduce traffic congestion, and strengthen connections within their school communities. The program is a partnership between [Safe Routes to School (SRTS)](https://www.austintexas.gov/saferoutes), [Get There ATX](https://www.austintexas.gov/department/transportation-demand-management), and [Ghisallo Cycling Initiative](https://ghisallo.org/).
What is a Bike Bus?
A Bike Bus is a group ride to and/or from school made up of students, families, and community members, traveling together along a fixed route. **Key roles for adults supporting a Bike Bus:**

items: Front Leader – sets the pace and navigates the route
Sweep Leader – monitors safety and watches for gaps
Rear Leader – keeps the group together and supports join-in riders

body.text: The 3 Cs of a Bike Bus​

Bike Buses are unique to each school community. The 3 Cs of a Bike Bus are at the core of launching a successful bike bus program. Keep these core principles in mind as you plan your school’s bike bus. ​
Community: The Foundation of Bike Buses. ​
Who will form your core planning team? Consider the following for your core team:​

items: Parents, guardians, and students.​
Who already bikes to school? ​
Teachers, PE coaches, and administration. ​
PTA and community partners.

body.text: ​Communication: Talk the Talk, before Biking the Bike.​
Communication helps you recruit your core team, engage others, and understand the needs of students and families. ​
Questions to consider: ​

items: How will the core team communicate? ​
Who will lead outreach? ​
How does your school community share information? ​
Does your PTA have a communication platform?

body.text: Consistency: Creating a Bike Culture​
Bike Buses that run consistently help bring neighbors together regularly. So, no matter how often, a regularly scheduled group ride can become a neighborhood social asset. ​

items: Daily, weekly, monthly, or once a semester. ​
Create the schedule that works for your community.​

body.text: Bike Buses Come in Different Formats:
Morning Only
Operates before school
Daily
Round-trip service on school days
Seasonal
Runs in fall and spring
Year Round
Operates most of the school year, weather permitting
Bike Bus Stop
A predetermined location that is either at the start of the route or a fixed point along the route.
Join-in Style
Students join the ride as it passes their location
How to Start a Bike Bus at Your School
Phase 0: Community Needs Assessment
Starting a bike bus is like planning the cake for a birthday party. You have an idea of what the birthday cake will look like, but you need to start by knowing what you have to work with. ​
We know that not all schools are equal; there are different needs within each community. By assessing your community’s needs, you can determine which resources are required to launch a bike bus. ​
Shopping List
Student needs may include:

items: Helmets
Functional Bike
Learning how to ride a bike (3rd- 8th grade)

body.text: Community Education about Bike Buses is needed.
Ingredients

items: Some established Bike Lanes, Shared Streets, and/or Trails​
High number of student who own helmet and/or bikes​
Desire within the PTA to start a Bike Bus ​

body.text: Cake and Icing

items: Protected Bike Lanes, Shared Streets, and/ or Trails lead to School
High number of students and families biking to school
Bike culture is present with the school community

body.text: Phase 1: Determine your Style
Daily Bike Bus:

The Safe Routes to School Crossing Guard Program is hiring Bike Bus Leaders only for schools that operate daily, mornings and afternoons, following the school’s schedule. Paid Bike Bus Leaders to have a criminal background check and complete Bike Bus Leader training.
Volunteer Bike Bus:
More flexibility, choose the style of Bike Bus that works for your school’s community. Whether weekly or monthly, consistency is key to starting a Bike Bus.
Phase 2: Recruit Leaders

items: Recruit at least three committed adults:
Lead Rider
Sweep Rider
Rear Rider
Daily Bike Bus Leaders must complete a criminal background check before being hired and trained.

body.text: Phase 3: Plan the Route

items: Map student locations
Choose safe, low-traffic streets
Test ride and adjust for safety

body.text: Phase 4: Prepare for Launch

items: Train leaders and prepare students/guardians
Collect waivers and emergency contacts
Establish communication channel (Google Groups, Discord, WhatsApp, PTA)
Promote via flyers, school channels, and parent groups
Request free safety gear from Get There ATX and SRTS

body.text: Phase 5: Launch & Operate

items: Soft launch 1–2 weeks before First Ride Day
Keep rides fun and consistent schedule
Maintain communication and follow weather policy

body.text: Phase 6: Evaluate & Grow

items: Collect feedback after launch
Adjust routes and expand as needed
Recruit more leaders and volunteers
Ongoing Bike Bus Leader training clinics available

Bike Bus Trainees putting on Helmets

body.text: Bike Bus Training Clinics

Curious about leading a Bike Bus or just want to learn more about safe group biking? Join one of our free, hands-on training clinics—they’re fun, informative, and open to anyone who wants to support active transportation in Austin schools.

These clinics are made possible by [Get There ATX](https://www.austintexas.gov/department/transportation-demand-management), [Safe Routes to School (SRTS)](https://www.austintexas.gov/saferoutes), and [Ghisallo Cycling Initiative](https://ghisallo.org/).
What you’ll learn:

items: The ABCs of bike safety
How to properly fit a helmet (yes, there’s a 5-step method!)
What each Bike Bus Leader does—Lead, Sweep, and Rear
How to communicate while riding (like calling out turns or stops)
Practice ride with role rotation
Q&A with City of Austin staff about the Bike Bus Pilot

body.text: Who should come? Parents, teachers, school staff, and community members who love biking and want to help students ride safely to school.

**Heads up:** Attending a clinic doesn’t automatically make you a paid Bike Bus Leader. To be hired, you’ll need to apply through the Safe Routes to School Crossing Guard program, pass a background check, and complete onboarding.
Get Involved & Learn More
Interest Form:
Sign up to become a Bike Bus Leader or attend a training clinic.

items: [Starting a Bike Bus](https://www.bikebuspdx.org/starting-a-bike-bus)
[Start a Bike Bus — Bike Bus World](https://bikebus.world/how-to-start-a-bike-bus)
[How to Start a Bike Bus: A Step-by-Step Guide for Families and Schools | PeopleForBikes](https://www.peopleforbikes.org/news/how-to-start-a-bike-bus-a-step-by-step-guide-for-f)
[Oregon Safe Routes to School Bike Bus Toolkit](https://oregonsaferoutes.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/ODOT-SRTS-Bike-Bus-Toolkit_v8.pdf)

body.text: Frequently Asked Questions
What are the benefits?
Improved health, focus, confidence, and reduced traffic around schools.
Who can be a Bike Bus Leader?
Anyone with a bike and helmet! Paid leaders must pass a background check, attend training, and support morning and afternoons rides following their school’s schedule.
Can my school participate?
Yes — with at least 3–5 leaders and support from school staff and PTA. We offer support to Volunteer and Daily Bike Buses.
Do I need to apply to attend training?
No. Clinics are open to all, but paid leaders must apply through SRTS Crossing Guard Program.
Why apply through SRTS?
It’s the current pathway for paid Bike Bus Leaders. Future processes may change.
Can my school request safety materials without a Bike Bus Leader?
Yes! Email [GetThereATX@AustinTexas.gov](mailto:GetThereATX@AustinTexas.gov) for bike maps, lights, and stickers.
When can my child ride alone?
Riding independence grows as experience and confidence grows. K–2 students should begin by riding with a guardian. Older students may ride independently.
Questions or want to learn more?
Email [GetThereATX@austintexas.gov](mailto:GetThereATX@austintexas.gov) for details or help getting started.

body.text: he Austin Public Library and Get There ATX officially launched their brand‑new **Bike Tool Loan Program** on **May 15, 2026** on **Bike to Work Day**. If you need to pump a tire, tighten a bolt or patch a tube on the fly, all you need is your library card to access your new favorite library perk.

The Austin Public Library and Get There ATX — the transportation demand management program of Austin Transportation and Public Works — collaborated to make this pilot possible. Over the next year, the team will track how the tools are used, host community events like Bike Fix‑It Clinics, and explore whether the service should expand to additional branches.

The Bike Tool Loan Program is at nine locations and will be equipped with everything you need for quick fixes and everyday maintenance. Pumps and patch kits will also be available, making it easy to keep your ride rolling smoothly.

It’s a simple idea with a big community payoff: give people the tools they need, remove barriers to biking, and help Austin stay active and connected. All tools, locks and bike pumps are for on-site use only.

summary.en: Planning a bike ride in Austin is simple with the city’s official Austin Bike Map. The map shows recommended bike routes all over the city (and beyond) and sorts them…

image.alt: Image of Bike Maps and Get There ATX Swag

body.text: Planning a bike ride in Austin is simple with the city’s official Austin Bike Map. The map shows recommended bike routes all over the city (and beyond) and sorts them by how comfortable they are to ride. This helps you choose the route that matches your skill level and what you enjoy.
Online Access

You can find the Austin Bike Map [online](https://austin.maps.arcgis.com/apps/webappviewer/index.html?id=c7fecf32a2d946fabdf062285d58d40c&extent=3052120.7123%2C10036958.1486%2C3179054.0456%2C10097891.4819%2C102739), and it’s updated regularly when new routes or improvements are added. The digital map makes it easy to look at different options before you start your ride, whether you’re going to work, getting some exercise or just having fun.
[Austin Bike Routes](https://austin.maps.arcgis.com/apps/webappviewer/index.html?id=c7fecf32a2d946fabdf062285d58d40c&extent=3052120.7123%2C10036958.1486%2C3179054.0456%2C10097891.4819%2C102739)
Please email bicycle@austintexas.gov if you have any questions.
Request Bike Maps

If you prefer a paper map, you can pick up a free printed Austin Bike Map at Austin City Hall. Each map has a QR code that links to the online version, so you can always check for changes along routes.
You can request a bulk order by emailing [**GetThereATX@austintexas.gov**](mailto:GetThereATX@austintexas.gov).
This is helpful whether you’re new to biking in Austin or planning your next big ride.

Disclaimer: This map illustrates popular bicycle routes that have been identified by the City of Austin. The City of Austin assumes no liability for bicyclists traveling on these routes and therefore bicyclists assume a risk while using these routes identical to the risks assumed on all other roadways.

summary.en: Austin proudly unveils the Wishbone Bridge and Unity Underpass, completing the lake-level loop of the Ann & Roy Butler Hike-and-Bike Trail. This milestone connects East Austin neighborhoods with scenic views,…

image.alt: Crowd gathers on Austin's wishbone bridge moments after its grand opening.

body.text: Austin proudly unveils the Wishbone Bridge and Unity Underpass, completing the lake-level loop of the Ann & Roy Butler Hike-and-Bike Trail. This milestone connects East Austin neighborhoods with scenic views, safe pathways, and vibrant public art. Below is a link to the custom 12″ x 18″ poster celebrating the event.

body.alt: Poster celebrating the opening of Austin's wishbone bridge and unity underpass.
body.caption: Poster celebrating the opening of Austin’s wishbone bridge and unity underpass.

body.text: [Download the poster](https://www.getthereatx.com/wishbone-bridge-poster/wishbone_bridge_poster_12x18-compressed_2026-02-07/)
Wishbone Bridge:

items: Austin’s first three-legged pedestrian bridge
1,087 feet long—longer than three football fields
Y-shaped design offering panoramic skyline and lake views

body.text: Unity Underpass:

items: Expands access 30x larger than the old culvert
Features “Absolute Equality: Unity Tunnel” artwork by Reginald C. Adams, spanning 5,000 sq. ft. with mosaics and murals
Reflects East Austin’s diversity and history

body.text: The completion of the Wishbone Bridge and Unity Underpass represents a major step forward in Austin’s commitment to connectivity, equity, and sustainability. Funded through the 2020 Mobility Bond and supported by a $4.1 million federal earmark secured by Rep. Greg Casar, this project closes a critical gap in the Ann & Roy Butler Hike-and-Bike Trail, creating a safe, scenic and accessible route for pedestrians and cyclists. Linking East Austin neighborhoods to the broader trail network promotes active transportation, health and community engagement while reducing reliance on cars. The project was delivered four months ahead of schedule and on budget, demonstrating efficient use of public resources.

Beyond functionality, it elevates the experience with art and design that reflect East Austin’s rich cultural heritage, and includes enhancements such as the Skyline Overlook, opening soon. Together, these features make the Wishbone Bridge and Unity Underpass not just infrastructure, but a symbol of progress and unity for all Austinites.

title.en: How Traffic Congestion Affects Air Quality

summary.en: Mental fatigue, irritability and increased stress are not the only side effect of sitting in traffic. In its 2024 Annual Report, Movability – Central Texas’ Transportation Management Association – found…

image.alt: Group of cyclists using a paved path with green space containing wildflowers between them and Mopac traffic

body.text: Mental fatigue, irritability and increased stress are not the only
side effect of sitting in traffic
. In its 2024 Annual Report,
Movability
– Central Texas’ Transportation Management Association – found traffic congestion costs a driver
$698 and 39 hours of sitting in traffic every year.

When there’s traffic congestion, cars slowly crawling along roadways — or not moving at all — there’s idling cars still running their engines. An idling vehicle emits pollutants such as carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and tiny particles that can harm our lungs and impact air quality.
Studies

have found that the vehicle technology put in place to prevent harmful pollutants from being released as exhaust. The type of vehicle and its age can change what kind of pollutants are being released into the air from the car’s exhaust. Some of the pollutants that impact air quality, like dust or soot (black exhaust), can get deep into our lungs. Even on clear days, some exhaust pollutants remain invisible to the eye but still impact our health. When sitting in traffic, you expose yourself to exhaust pollutions that over time increase your risk of developing asthma and breathing problems, heart disease, lung cancer, stroke or premature death.
Who are most at risk?

items: Commuters sitting in their idling vehicles
Professional drivers, like truck drivers and bus drivers
People who live or work near major highways or busy roads
Children, seniors, and those who are most sensitive to pollution

body.text: Is this the new normal? Is poor air quality inevitable?
This is Austin, we are meant to be weird!
So, let’s not let poor air quality be normal. We might not get rid of vehicle exhaust overnight, but we can reimagine how we commute!
Reducing transportation emissions by building a more multimodal travel culture is certainly the ultimate solution to
traffic congestion pollution

and improving local air quality. When you switch your commute to walking, biking, scooting, carpooling and using public transit, you save money, enjoy your commute more, reduce traffic congestion and contribute to cleaner air!
Start small. Use resources like Get There ATX (GTATX) and
Movability
to see what options work for you. They offer help planning solutions to help make your commute a little weirder, like:

items: Carpooling with a coworker on days when you’re working the same hours
Riding your bike on a short trip close to your home two times a week – short 1-3 mile trips are the majority of trips in Central Texas – Every non-driving trip not taken is fewer emissions
Taking public transit three times per month to events, appointments, or to work or school

body.text: Find out how much
you can save
and reduce emissions on the GTATX Trip Planner! These resources are supported by
MyCommute Solutions

summary.en: Our interactive map highlights rideshare drop-off and pickup locations, detours, bike parking areas, public restrooms, and more for the Spring Festival Season.

image.alt: Two people waiting to board the Metro Rail

body.text: We’ve got your one-stop shop for getting around during the Spring Festival Season! Check out this [interactive map](https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/119f8c50fe65408584f8150d2702d5fb/page/Mobility-Guide/) highlighting rideshare drop-off and pickup locations, detours, bike parking areas, public restrooms, and more.
Want some quick tips? Here’s how to beat traffic during Austin’s Spring Festival Season, whether you’re a local or you’re in town for the festival:

items: Work from home if possible to avoid traffic, especially if you work downtown.
Avoid [pedestrian-only zones](https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/119f8c50fe65408584f8150d2702d5fb/page/Mobility-Guide/) if you’re driving a car, riding a bike or using a scooter.

Follow scooter etiquette, such as parking in designated areas and picking up any knocked-over devices. Brush up on etiquette [here](https://www.austintexas.gov/page/bicycle-and-micromobility-laws-and-safety).

Take the [CapMetro Rail](https://www.capmetro.org/rail) or [Bus](https://www.capmetro.org/ourservices/busroutes) downtown instead of driving, as parking is expensive and hard to find. Plan your CapMetro trip [here](https://www.capmetro.org/planner).
Don’t drink and drive. The City of Austin offers safe ride options and parking ticket forgiveness. Learn more options to get home safe [here](https://www.austintexas.gov/gethomesafely).
